title: Social Conditions and Land Revenue Systems during Asafjahi Rule

concepts.bodyMd:
*   Nizam-ul-Mulk Asafjah separated the Deccan from the Mughal Empire, ruling under his own centralized control while nominally retaining regard for the Mughals.
*   Appointed Mansabdars without Mughal consent — his own Mansabdars were called **"Aasifias"**.
*   His heirs did not continue Mughal traditions.
*   Capital shifted from **Aurangabad to Hyderabad in 1764**.
*   **1724–1762**: internal conflicts among heirs shaped State formation.
*   **1762–1803**: **Nizam Ali Khan's** reign brought internal stability — expansion of forts, army, and administrative buildings.
*   The resulting upper administrative class was called **Stately Officers (Prabhuvargam)**.

### Jagirdari System

*   **Jagir** meant a right ensuring permanent income through land — the practice of honoring persons for army-related service.
*   One-third of the State was held as Jagirs.
*   Big landlords (**Jagirdars**) collected taxes independently, with civic and judicial powers.
*   Upper-level rulers' council: **Umra-E-Ajam**.
*   No uniform classification of ranks — due to (1) lack of standard classification and (2) heredity-based ownership.
*   Standing depended on: (1) military service/relation with Nizam, (2) court reputation.
*   Under Mohammedan rule, Jagir = owning landed property (also called **Inam, Altamshoo, Madaa-e-Maash**).

**Threefold division of Hyderabad land:**

| Division | Description |
|---|---|
| Jagirdari | Land-owning/non-land-owning, held by Stately Officers |
| Sarfekhaas | Lands belonging to the King (Nizam) |
| Dewani | Government lands |

*   Jagirdari + Sarfekhaas = held by Stately Officers; Dewani formed two-thirds of total land.
*   Stately Officers' land, four parts: **Sarfekhaas, Pygah** (maintaining King's forces), **Jagirs**, **Samsthanams** (pre-Nizam Hindu kingdoms/feudatories).

**Social hierarchy (highest to lowest):** King → Pygah nobles → Umar-E-Ajam/Samsthanaadheeswaras (Stately Officers) → Jagirdars (big/middle/small) → I & II class Govt. employees → III class employees/traders → IV class employees/labourers.

*   Hereditary position; held titles like **Raja, Maharaja, Deshmukh, Sardar, Nawab, Reddy, Chowdhury**.
*   Collected taxes, kept peasants under control; some held independent/sovereign status in their Jagirs.

*   **Vatandari**: cultivator-as-landowner system (Bhookamatamu), ancient, held by local landowners: **Patels, Patwaris, Deshmukhs, Sardeshmukhs, Deshpandes, Sardeshpandes**.
*   Under **Salaar Jung's** revenue reforms, Patels/Patwaris got land titles (**Pattas**) and cash pay.
*   **Deshmukhs and Deshpandes** were the revenue authorities of the Paraganas (provinces).
*   After the **Zilaabandi system**, Paragana authorities lost these responsibilities and land grants.
*   **Rusum-e-Zamindari**: 5% (Deshmukhs) + 2½% (Deshpandes) of collected taxes, paid as hereditary service fee.
*   **'Omlis'**: fixed taxes regardless of actual collection (mainly Karnataka region); 2/3 went to Government.
*   **'Sera'/'savaram'**: free land grants to Deshmukhs/Deshpandes for service.
*   **Reddys**: high-pedigreed landowners, also called Deshmukhs, Deshpandes, or **'Dora'/'Desai'**; British employed them as tax collectors and soldiers.
*   **Raj Bahadur Venkat Ram Reddy**: first Hindu Kotwal of Hyderabad (1920s), served 14 years.
*   Zamindars who fought against the Nizam (armed struggle from **1946**): **Ravi Narayana Reddy, Laxmi Narayana Reddy, Kodanda Rami Reddy, Baddam Ella Reddy**.

*   **Gadi** (Fort) — term confined to Telangana; built of sand and lime; Zamindars held court there with family.
*   Doras kept horses (some used cars); joint family system; village Zamindars also called **Jagirdars/Maktedars**.
*   Icons of village Doras: **Nawab Salar Jung, Maharaja Kishan Parshad, Nawab Kamal Jung**.
*   Lack of education → unbridled Patel/Patwari authority; **Karanams** (addressed as "Patwaris") held complete land-holding knowledge.
*   **95% of Deshmukhs were Reddys; 95% of Deshpandes were Brahmins** — yet no matrimonial ties between the groups.
*   **Zamindars wielded more authority than the Kings.**

*   Hyderabad was religiously/culturally mixed — **"Ganga Jamuna Tehjeeb"**.
*   **1881 census**: 90.32% Hindu, 9.40% Muslim, 0.09% Christian, 0.08% Jain, 0.06% Parsi, 0.0031% Sikh, 47 Jews.
*   By **1911 census**, Hindu % decreased, Muslim % increased in the city overall, but villages stayed more Hindu.
*   Caste order: **Brahmins → Kshatriyas → Vaishyas → Shudras** (originally 4, expanded to hundreds).

**Brahmins**: Two branches — Dravida, Gowda; by practice — Vaishnavas (Vishnu), Smarthas (Shiva); by occupation — **Vaidika** (priests/astrologers, poor) and **Niyogi** (army/agriculture/business; became **Karanams**, Sub Collectors, Translators under British).

**Kshatriyas**: Second position; wore sacred threads; observed purdah; branches — Surya, Chandra, Matsya Vamsha; shifted to agriculture.

**Vaishyas**: Third position; commerce/trade; **Komatis** in Andhra/Telangana; also money-lending; vegetarians.

**Shudras**: Fourth, majority population; agriculture; many occupational sub-castes.

**Caste-by-occupation table:**

| Class | Castes |
|---|---|
| Agricultural | Kapu, Reddy, Velama, Kamma |
| Animal-tending | Golla, Jalagari, Besta, Boya |
| Panchannam vaaru | Vadrangi, Gayadla, Pinjaari, Chitrakarulu, Jogata, Netavaru, Salevaru, Vannegallu |
| Trading | Komati, Balija, Telaga, Perika, Gandlavaaru |
| Service | Chakali, Mangali, Katika, Katipapala, Medara, Idiga, Talari, Masti, Jetti, Chatri, Charma Karulu |
| Poojari | Brahmins, Jangalu, Lingayats, Janagalu, Jogulu, Jatadharulu |
| Dependent | Picchakuntla, Bhavanas, Runjulu, Pambalulu, Budabukkalu, Bhattu, Chandala, Maatangulu, Kommuri Dasas, Taviri Dasas, Suddulu |
| Entertaining | Dommari, Bhogamvaaru, Vipra vinodulu, Aindrajaalikulu, Bommalaatala vaaru |
| Avadhoota | Paramahamsas, Sanyasulu, Satani, Sivasattulu, Tambala, Yogulu, Jaina, Veera mushti, Kaleparasulu |
| Asprusyulu | Mala, Madiga, Adihindu, Maliar, Mehatar, Chambaar, Mochi |
| Girijanulu (Tribal) | Chenchu, Boya, Yaanadi, Gond, Pavara, Koli, Erukala, Lambadi, Bhil, Koya, Kondaredlu |
| Videseeyulu (Foreign) | Parangulu, Ingileesulu, Paraasulu, Turaka, Odde, Gurjapu, Gowda, Mesra |

**Key caste notes:**

*   **Kapus/Reddys**: cultivating landowners; sub-sects Patangi, Motati, Udati, Pedakanti, Aare, Kamma, Velama, Konda, Aadi, Gona, Konidi.
*   **Velamas**: North Indian immigrant origin; leaders called **Samasthanaadeswaras**.
*   **Kammas**: agriculturists, claim Kshatriya status; women observe Ghosha.
*   **Panchanamvaaru** (Vishwakarma lineage): Vadrangi (carpenter), Kamsaali (goldsmith — most important), Kasevaru (sculptor), Kammarulu (iron), Kancharulu (brass).
*   **Kummari**: potters; village elders (Ayagars).
*   **Salevaru** (weavers): sub-castes — Devanga, Togata, Padmasaali (weaving), Pattusaali (silk), Devangas (cotton), Togata (zari); deity Yellamma/Renukamaata.
*   **Mangali (Barber)**: called **Nayee Brahmins**; women did midwifery, men surgery.
*   **Gollas**: animal husbandry, also known as Yadavas.
*   **Idiga/Goundla**: toddy extraction, low social rung.
*   **Telagas**: soldiers under Golconda/Qutub Shahi rulers, called Batroths; till 1870 mostly worked as Deshmukh troops.
*   **Asprusyulu (Untouchables)**: Parahaa caste, 5th position; lived outside villages.
*   **Mala**: agricultural labourers; ate meat, didn't visit Hindu temples.
*   **Madiga**: hide-cleaning/chappal-making.
*   **Adivasis**: Chenchus (villages), Koyas (forests) — Koya language; 6th category.
*   **Gonds**: warrior class, Adilabad forests, ruled **1240–1750**.
*   **Erukalu**: known for robbery/crime; women (Erukala Saanulu) did divination.
*   **Lambadies ('Sugle'/'Banjaras')**: migrated from Rajasthan, sold salt.
*   **Balotadars**: village servants (priest, carpenter, blacksmith, potter, washerman, barber, Madiga, Mala) paid in paddy ("Balota") for service; included Karanam, Patel.
*   **Muslims**: arrived 14th century; Shia/Sunni; foreign-origin called **'Afaakies'**, local called **'Deccanis'**; mostly army/administration/commerce.
*   **Dodekula caste**: Hindu-to-Islam converts, spoke Telugu.
*   **Europeans**: traded from Machilipatnam, Yanam, Ganjam, Narsapur, Kakinada.
*   **Looso Indians**: Portuguese-Deccan hybrid race.

*   Hyderabad: 6th-biggest princely state, 17 million population; culture called **'Ganga Jamuna Tehjeeb'**.
*   Women's condition studied in **three phases**: (1) first Nizam to 19th century, (2) intermediate reform period, (3) 20th century.

**Phase 1** (worst period, till Salar Jung I's appointment as PM):

*   Women confined to four walls; even royal/rich women lacked individual liberty.
*   Outside this norm: **Ayahs, Dayaas** (harem servants), **Tawaifs** (dancers — NOT prostitutes, respected artistes), and **Harlots** (practiced prostitution, socially disrespected).
*   Nizam maintained Tawaifs via office **'Daftar-e-Arab Nishat'**, spending **Rs. 11,000** on salaries.
*   **Purdah** was rampant among pedigreed families; unmarried daughters of the Nizam were exempt.

**Notable women (Phase 1):**

*   **Qairunnisa Begum**: married British Resident **Kirkpatrick**; Nizam adopted Kirkpatrick as son, title **'Hashmat Jung Bahadur'**; residency built became **Govt. Women's College**.
*   **Mahalakha Chandabai** (b.1766): first Urdu poetess of India; title **'Umrao'**; pen name **Chanda**; poems published 1824 as **'Guljar-e-Mahalakha'**; 125 Ghazals preserved in British Museum; died in the **1824 famine**.

**Phase 2** (**1853–1883**): **Salar Jung** as PM; first Primary School for girls started; reduction in child marriages; seeds of women's education sown.

**Prominent women (18th–20th c.) — key facts:**

*   **Sowgra Humayun Mirza** (b.1882): founded **Anjuman-E-Khavaateen Deccan**; started Safdaria Girls School.
*   **Tayyaba Begum Sahiba Bilgrami** (b.1873): **first woman in India to get a B.A. degree** (1910, Madras University).
*   **Tayyaba Begum**: founded first **Arts & Crafts School** and first **Domestic Science College** in Hyderabad.
*   **Sarojini Naidu** (b.1879): "**Bul-bul-E-Hind**"; wrote _The Golden Threshold_, _The Bird of Time_; President of INC (Kanpur, 1925); **Kaizar-E-Hind medal**; Governor of West Bengal post-independence; fought purdah and child marriage; poem **'Tears of Asaf'** on Musi floods.

**Women's education milestones:**

*   **1907**: Janana school for Muslim girls started (Sixth Nizam); **79 schools by 1930**.
*   **1898**: **'Tahajib-un-Nisan'** paper by Sayyed Mumtaz Ali & Mohammadi Begum.
*   **1904**: **'Khatoon'** paper by Sheik Abdullah Hadis & Jahana Begum, Aligarh.
*   **Mir Osman Ali Khan** (25-year rule): established **677 primary, 28 middle, 4 special training schools**.
*   **1938**: Domestic Science syllabus introduced for women.
*   **Madapati Hanumantha Rao**: started a Girls School in Narayanaguda.

**Women in Independence Movement (key names & roles):**

*   **Jnana Kumari Heda**: first Satyagrahi from Hyderabad State.
*   **T. Varalakshmamma**: President, 2nd Andhra Mahila Sabha; started Women Health Education Parishad.
*   **Nadimpalli Sundaramma**: founded **Andhra Sodari Samajam (1915)**.
*   **Arutla Kamaladevi**: first woman opposition leader of a State (Deputy Leader, Communist Party, 1962).
*   **Sangem Lakshmibayamma**: only woman jailed for the National movement; first-generation Telangana graduate; later Lok Sabha member from Medak.

**Organizations:**

*   First women's society: **Bharata Mahila Samajam (1907)**.
*   **Andhra Sodari Samajam (1925)**, **Andhra Mahila Sabha (1930)**, **Andhra Yuvati Mandali (1935)**.

**Prominent Ladies (key facts only):**

*   **Princess Durru Shevar**: last Ottoman heir; established Hyderabad's first Airport, Osmania General Hospital.
*   **Nilofeur**: last Ottoman princess; built Nilofeur Hospital; did not observe purdah.
*   **Masuma Begum**: **first Muslim lady to become a Minister in India** (1960).

Main evils: **bonded-labour, bagela, begari, illiteracy, child marriages, polygamy, dowry, purdah, Jogini system, prostitution.**

### Bonded Labour

*   Confined to tribals/backward castes in theory, but rampant across Telangana society.
*   Harijan families forced to spare a member for unpaid service to Patel, Patwari, Karanam, Deshmukhs.
*   Numerous free-service obligations: toddy, cloth, tools, washing, transport, food, and — most heinous — sending girls into service at landlord weddings.
*   **Jagirdars, Zamindars, Paigahs, Samsthanaadheeswaras** collected ~**Rs. 10 crores** in illegal taxes (State's lawful revenue before 1940 was ~**Rs. 8 crores**).
*   Example: **Visunoor Ramchandrareddy** (Deshmukh, Janagaon) controlled bonded labour across ~40 villages.
*   **Armed struggle in Telangana began in 1946** due to such excesses.
*   **Mir Osman Ali Khan prohibited Begar in 1911**; law helped end bonded labour only with 20th-century education/reform.

### Bagela

*   Peasant unable to pay taxes became a bonded servant of the landlord.
*   Prevalent in **Nalgonda and Warangal** districts.
*   Debt passed to heirs if unpaid in lifetime.
*   **Abolished by Nizam Government in 1930.**

### Begari

*   Forced unpaid labour, in vogue since ancient times, in towns and villages alike.
*   **1911**: Osman Ali Khan's farmana to abolish — ineffective.
*   **1922 Farmana**: wages fixed (12 seers paddy/men, 8/women, 6/children); children under 10 exempted.
*   **Abolished with Nizam's merger into Indian Union, 1948.**

### Child Marriages

*   More common among Hindus (especially Brahmins) than Muslims; none among Christians.
*   Caused: poverty, illiteracy; led to health issues/early death.
*   **1899**: Age of Consent for Marriage Act.
*   **Sarada Act, 1930**: abolished child marriage.

### Widow Marriages

*   Common in lower castes, rare in upper castes; Nizam State had **4x more widows than widowers**.
*   **Widow Remarriage Act, 1856** — never enforced.
*   **Salar Jung** married a widow, setting an example.

### Polygamy

*   Muslim Shariat permitted up to **4 wives**; upper-caste Hindu men also practiced it. Women could not remarry.
*   Declined due to social reform and 20th-century Government efforts.

### Dowry

*   **Varasulkam** (dowry to bridegroom's family) more common in Telangana than **Kanyasulkam** (dowry to bride's family).
*   Most prevalent among **Reddys and Velamas**; still continues today.

### Devadasi–Jogini System

*   Temple girls dedicated to God (Devadasis), later exploited by landlords — evolved into the **Jogini system**, mainly in North Telangana.
*   Abolished due to reform efforts (Raghupati Venkata Ramiah Naidu in Andhra; Andhra Maha Sabha/Yuvati Mandali in Telangana).

### Aadapapa

*   Girls kept as bonded slaves/concubines by rulers and Zamindars, mostly in lower castes; children also became Aadapapas.

### Prostitution

*   Encouraged by Nawabs/rulers; performers called **'Tawaiffs'**.
*   Office: **'Daftar-E-Nishan Kanchen Kacheris'**; supervisor titled **'Mamasharifa'**.
*   This Tawaif system was **unique to Telangana, not found in Andhra**.

### Purdah

*   Spread from North India by Muslims; adopted by Hindu elites too.
*   Entered Telangana **during Qutub Shahi period**, continued under Asafjahis.
*   Survives today mainly in Muslim families.

* * *

# Land Tenures and Land Revenue Systems during Asafjahi Rule

Land Tenures and Land Revenue Systems during Asafjahi Rule — as Hyderabad State was essentially agriculture-based, land ownership shaped both livelihoods and social standing.  

*   **68% of population** depended on agriculture; land ownership = social status marker.
*   Land revenue formed **50.29% of total tax revenue** (1933–34).

### Land Classification

1.  **Diwani/Khalsa lands** — direct Govt. administration; **54.8%** of State's 82,698 sq. miles.
2.  **Non-Khalsa lands** (**45.2%**) — (a) **Sarf-I-Khas** (Nizam's privy purse), (b) **Jagir/Inam** grants.

**Table: Types of Land Tenures**

| Diwani/Khalsa | Other Khalsa Tenures | Non-Khalsa |
|---|---|---|
| Ryotwari (Pattedari, Pot-Pattedari, Shikmidari, Asami Shikmi) | Pan-Maqta; Tahud/Sarbasta; Ijara; Agrahar | Sarf-I-Khas; Samsthan/Peshkash; Jagir (Paigah, Al-Tamgha, Zat, Tankha, Mashrooti, Madad Mash); Inam |

*   **Ryotwari tenure** (Bombay-system based): most important — over **50% of area**, more than **20 million acres**.
*   Pattedar keeps land as long as revenue paid; evictable only for public purpose with compensation.

### Cultivating Tenures & Tenants

*   **Pattedari**: simple occupancy (self/hired cultivation).
*   **Pot-Pattedari**: joint-stock cultivation, equal rights, not much in vogue.
*   **Shikmidari**: land handed to cultivators (Shikmidars) under agreement — protected tenants.
*   **Asami-Shikmi**: tenants-at-will; became Shikmidar after 12 years' continuous occupation.
*   Most leases (**75%**) were oral, tenancies-at-will terminated yearly — landlords avoided written agreements to prevent tenant rights.
*   **Committee (1940) → Asami-Shikmi Act (1945)** → operative 1947 — recognized 6-year continuous occupants (1933–43) as protected tenants; poorly implemented.
*   Non-Ryotwari tenures (Jagir, Maqta, Ijara, Agrahar, Inam) had even worse tenant conditions — cultivators of up to **90 years' standing** still treated as tenants-at-will.
*   **1,137 of 5,800 non-Diwani villages** remained unsurveyed by 1949, enabling record manipulation by landlords.
*   **Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 10 June 1950** — finally secured tenant rights (implemented post-1950).

### Other Khalsa Tenures

*   **Pan-Maqta**: contract tenure, fixed quit-rent, permanent/life grants; Maqtedars behaved like Jagirdars, manipulating records via Patel/Patwari posts they held.
*   **Tahud/Sarbasta/Watandari**: tax-farming system; **abolished by Salar Jung I in 1866**. Ex-tax-farmers (Deshmukhs/Deshpandyas) compensated with land, strengthening their position.
    *   **Rusum-i-zamindari**: hereditary pension = **7½%** of revenue (5% Deshmukhs, 2½% Deshpandyas), no service required.
    *   Village-level Watandars: Patels, Patwaris, Talari, Sethsindhi, Neredu, Dhein.
*   **Ijara** (1878): land-development lease, light rates rising to full assessment over **5–40 years**; abolished **1909 (1318 Fasli)**.
*   **Agrahara**: quit-rent tenure for religious institutions; in practice, absentee landlordism and exploitation like other tenures.

### Sarf-I-Khas

*   **10% of Dominions**, spread over 18 Taluqs; Nizam's privy purse; administered by Diwani officials under **Sadar-ul-Moham**.
*   Miserly spending on welfare/irrigation despite good revenue collection; low staff salaries.
*   **Taken over by Government in February 1949.**

### Paigahs

*   **'Paigah'** = Persian for stable/cavalry; also **Jamiat Jagirs**; created by **Nizam Ali Khan (1761–1803)** as counter-balancing military force after Minister **Rukhnuddaula's** death (1775).
*   Over **1,000 villages**, 2,000+ sq. miles, across 237 Taluqs, 10 Districts; none in Nalgonda (poor soil/irrigation).
*   Full internal administrative/judicial control; **Reilly Commission (1927)** recommended disbanding — Nizam's **1929 Firman** rejected this.

### Jagirs

*   Introduced by **Nizam-ul-mulk**; 1/3rd of territory distributed to nobles (Muslims: military; Hindus: administration).
*   Types: **Al-tamgha** (revenue-free, permanent), **Zat** (unconditional maintenance grant), **Mashrooti** (service-conditional), **Madadmash** (gratuity/supplement), **Tankha** (pre-1853 salary substitute, redeemed by **Salar Jung I in 1853**).
*   **Exempted Jagirdars**: big Jagirdars; **222 in Medak Suba alone** — ran private governments (own courts, police, revenue, survey depts.) — "State within a State."
*   **Non-exempted Jagirs**: smaller, e.g., 531 in Medak Suba; paid **Haq-e-malikana royalty (2–25%)**.
*   Jagirdars collected **25–50% more revenue** than Khalsa villages; extracted **nazarana** before granting Pattedari rights.
*   **35 types of illegal cesses** existed (e.g., Shadi-Patti/marriage tax, Ghar-Patti/house tax, Mohtarfa/handloom tax, grazing fines).
*   **Vetti** (forced labour) was the most-hated practice — banned by Firman **1926**, ignored in practice.
*   Jagir administration neglected education (75% villages had no primary school) and health/irrigation.
*   Popular anger against Jagirdars fueled the **Peasants' Armed Struggle (1946–51)**.

### Inams

*   'Inam' (Arabic: favour/reward) — revenue-free/partial land grant for service, charity, or reward; often hereditary.
*   **Balota Inams**: 1/4th assessment, for village service.
*   **Inam Commission (1865–1912)** — validated/resumed fraudulent grants.
*   Total Inamdars: **83,000** (57,000 Diwani, 28,000 Jagir).
*   **Circular No.4, 1298 Fasli (1889)**: allowed Inamdars to legally occupy excess land — worsened land concentration.

### Samsthanas

*   **'Peshkash'**: fixed annual tribute paid by conquered rulers/chiefs in exchange for self-administration.
*   Only **3 true Peshkash Guzars**: **Gadwal (Rs.86,540), Anagundi (Rs.10,000), Gurgunta (Rs.7,050)**.
*   Pan-Maqta-style Peshkash payers: **Wanaparti, Gopalpet, Jatpol, Bhadrachalam**.

| Ruler | Peshkash |
|---|---|
| Wanaparti | Rs.83,862 |
| Jatpol | Rs.71,944 |
| Gopalpet | Rs.22,663 |
| Bhadrachalam | Rs.45,875 |
| **Total** | **Rs.2,13,844** |

*   **14 Samsthanas** total; only **5 exempted** from Diwani jurisdiction — 3 of these (**Gadwal, Wanaparti, Jatpol**) from Mahaboobnagar District.
*   Unlike scattered Jagirs, Samsthanas were **compact territorial units**, with own Police/Judicial systems and revenue surplus.
*   Some Samsthandars — **Raja Rameshwar Rao of Wanaparti (d.1922)**, **Raja Venkat Lachman Rao Bahadur of Jatpole (d.1929)** — were benevolent, modernizing rulers.

### Survey and Settlement

*   **Survey and Settlement Department established 1875** (post tax-farming abolition by Salar Jung I).
*   Bombay system adopted, adapted: Telangana rice areas assessed high in wet years, remitted in failure years (unlike Bombay's flat rate).
*   **Ayacut** (irrigable area) rule allowed corrupt over-classification as "wet land" — corrected only in **September 1949**.
*   Work began: **1899 (1298 Fasli)** in Medak/Nizamabad Taluqs; **1915–16** in Mahaboobnagar.
*   Settlement period: originally 30 years, reduced to **15 years** for Telangana.
*   **Record of Rights Act (1936)** — flawed, recognized only nominal Pattedars; replaced by a **new Act in 1949** recognizing actual land holders.

### Land Revenue Assessments

**Table: Rate of Assessment (1912–1945), Rs-Annas-Paisa**

| Division | Before 1912 Dry/Wet | 1912–22 Dry/Wet | 1934 Dry/Wet | 1945 Dry/Wet |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Marathwada | 0-13-10 / 5-0-9 | 1-0-1 / 5-8-4 | 1-1-11 / 5-15-5 | 1-2-2 / 9-12-3 |
| Telangana | 0-11-11 / 11-1-3 | 0-12-5 / 11-6-7 | 1-0-8 / 12-3-6 | 0-14-2 / 12-5-3 |
| **State Avg.** | 0-12-10 / 8-1-0 | 0-14-3 / 8-7-5 | 1-0-8 / 9-1-6 | 1-0-7 / 11-2-0 |

*   Assessment rates rose steadily 1912–1945; **dry land assessment higher in Marathwada, wet land assessment higher in Telangana**.
*   Telangana wet rate (Medak Suba: **Rs.23-0-0/acre**) was 3x higher than Madras State (**Rs.7-1-6**).
*   **S.M. Bharucha (1936–37 study)**: on a 16-acre farm, land revenue (Rs.30) was 9.4% of net yield (Rs.320), leaving little margin after other costs.
*   **50% extra rate** charged on tank-irrigated double-crop lands, discouraging second cropping.
*   **Mr. O'Connor** (Nizam's Govt.) suggested a **25–30% reduction** in land revenue — never implemented.

### Rents

*   **1901–1911**: rent-receivers increased **1,748.8%** — landlords shifted from owner-farming to renting out.
*   **Cash rents**: 40% of leased land (mainly dry land); risk borne by tenant; rents were **2–3x assessment rates** (tenants effectively paid 4–6x assessment).
*   **Batai** (crop-sharing, 50-50): mainly for wet lands; risk shared between landlord and tenant.
*   Rent burden: **35–45%** of produce (tank-irrigated), **25–30%** (well-irrigated), **15–40%** (dry, food vs cash crops).
*   **Famine Commission (1901)**: noted tenants had sunk to the condition of "mere serfs."

### Remissions

**Table: Remission Sub-heads, 1324 Fasli (1914–15)**

| Head | Marathwada % | Telangana % | Total % |
|---|---|---|---|
| Water excess/deficit | 0.8 | 35.5 | 36.3 |
| Breach of irrigation sources | 1.2 | 20.2 | 21.4 |
| Submergence before cultivation | 0.1 | 5.8 | 5.9 |
| Talaf Mal (crop failure) | 0.0 | 0.8 | 0.8 |
| Change of crop/irrigation | 0.2 | 19.3 | 19.5 |
| Double-crop cash remission | 0.5 | 8.8 | 9.3 |
| Other | 0.7 | 6.1 | 6.8 |
| **Total** | **3.5** | **96.5** | **100.0** |

*   Telangana got **96.5% of remissions** (wet/chalka soils); Marathwada only 3.5% (dry black-soil tracts).
*   Remissions mostly benefited **wet lands only**, and mainly wells built before **1908/1915** — corrected only in 1949.
*   In practice, remissions rarely helped actual cultivators — officials extracted "mamuls" (bribes) to process claims; big landlords benefited most.
*   **Sarf-I-Khas and Jagir villages** were denied remissions in practice, despite Government orders.

Land tenures and revenue administration in Hyderabad State were dominated by feudal, hereditary, authoritarian power groups (**Deshmukhs, Deshpandyas, Patels, Patwaris, Maqtedars, Agraharaiks, Paighas, Jagirdars, Samsthandars**). 

Diwani and non-Diwani tenures differed only in degree, not kind — both featured high assessments, rack-renting, forced/free labour (vetti), and remission systems that mainly benefited big landlords. Education, health, and infrastructure development in non-Diwani areas were minimal, with no channel for popular grievance redressal — conditions that fed directly into the **Telangana Peasants' Armed Struggle (1946–51)**.
